title.en: Spend the third dimension on information

summary: Use depth when it encodes a variable or a real spatial relationship, not to make a flat diagram look richer.
objective: Decide honestly whether a data scene benefits from being three-dimensional.
applies_when: An abstract diagram, graph or chart is being built in three dimensions.
Elements occlude each other or change apparent size with distance.
The viewer must compare values or trace connections.
intent_signals: the bars at the back are hidden
should this be a flat chart
example_prompts: Decide whether this system diagram benefits from three dimensions.
Lay out the graph so depth carries the hierarchy.
negative_signals: Genuinely spatial subjects such as buildings, terrain or molecules.
Scenes whose purpose is exploration and atmosphere rather than reading values.
not_for: Genuinely spatial subjects such as buildings, terrain or molecules.
Scenes whose purpose is exploration and atmosphere rather than reading values.

principles: Depth costs before it pays: it introduces occlusion, perspective scaling that distorts comparison, and a navigation burden, all of which apply even when the third axis carries nothing.

It earns its cost when the third axis encodes something real, such as time, hierarchy depth, a third variable, or a genuine spatial relationship, or when the interaction of moving through the data is the point.
Value comparison is the weakest use. Perspective makes equal quantities look different by position, which is exactly the comparison a chart exists to support.
The decision is not all or nothing: a three-dimensional scene can carry a flat, readable panel for the quantitative part.
implementation: Name what depth is doing before building: encoding a variable, expressing a real spatial relationship, or supporting exploration and atmosphere. Only the first two support quantitative reading. Decorative or experiential depth is a legitimate choice; what it must not do is invite a measurement it cannot support.
Where depth is used for a variable, provide an orthographic or aligned view so comparisons are not distorted by perspective.
Give the viewer a canonical viewpoint to return to, since arbitrary angles make a spatial layout unreadable.
Reduce occlusion structurally through layering, transparency or filtering rather than expecting the viewer to orbit.
Pair the spatial view with a flat panel for values that must be compared precisely.
observable_checks: Ask what depth is doing and check the scene against that answer: where it encodes a variable, confirm the reading is honest and undistorted; where it is exploratory or decorative, confirm no quantitative claim rests on it.
Compare two elements with equal values at different depths and see whether they read as equal.
Count how many elements are hidden from the default viewpoint.
Confirm a return-to-default view exists and that the default is the intended reading position.

creative_affordances: Spatial data worlds can be delightful and memorable; the rule asks for a reason, not for restraint.
Deliberately non-quantitative spatial metaphors are valid when precise reading is not claimed.
known_limits: Authored composition guidance; it cites no perceptual study and no user testing was performed.
No runtime scene has been evaluated for this record.
